findings.title: Missing Content Security Policy (CSP) Header
findings.description: The Content-Security-Policy (CSP) header is missing. This header helps mitigate cross-site scripting (XSS) and other content injection attacks by specifying which dynamic resources are allowed to load. Without it, the browser will load content from any source, making the application more vulnerable to client-side attacks.
findings.recommendation: Implement a strict Content Security Policy (CSP) header. Define trusted sources for scripts, styles, images, and other resources. For example: `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data:;` (adjust as needed for application functionality).

findings.title: Missing X-Frame-Options Header
findings.description: The X-Frame-Options header is not set. This header prevents clickjacking attacks by controlling whether a browser can render a page in a `<frame>`, `<iframe>`, `<embed>`, or `<object>` tag. Without this header, the page can be embedded on malicious sites, potentially leading to clickjacking.
findings.recommendation: Add the `X-Frame-Options` header to your web server configuration. Recommended values are `DENY` (prevents embedding by any site) or `SAMEORIGIN` (allows embedding only by sites from the same origin).

findings.title: Cookies Missing Secure and/or HttpOnly Flags
findings.description: One or more cookies are transmitted without the 'Secure' and/or 'HttpOnly' flags. The 'Secure' flag ensures cookies are only sent over HTTPS, preventing interception by passive network attackers. The 'HttpOnly' flag prevents client-side scripts from accessing the cookie, mitigating some XSS risks.
findings.recommendation: Ensure all sensitive cookies are set with both the 'Secure' and 'HttpOnly' flags. The 'Secure' flag should be used for all cookies on HTTPS sites. The 'HttpOnly' flag should be used for session management and authentication cookies.

findings.title: Information Disclosure in HTTP Headers
findings.description: The server is disclosing potentially sensitive information, such as the server type, version, or underlying technologies, in HTTP response headers (e.g., 'Server', 'X-Powered-By'). This information can be used by attackers to identify known vulnerabilities associated with specific software versions.
findings.recommendation: Configure the web server to suppress or generalize server-identifying headers (e.g., 'Server', 'X-Powered-By'). While not a direct vulnerability, reducing information disclosure is a security best practice.

findings.title: SQL Injection (Time-based Blind)
findings.description: The GET parameter 'id' at 'https://juice-shop.herokuapp.com/?id=1' is highly vulnerable to time-based blind SQL injection. This allows an unauthenticated attacker to extract arbitrary data from the underlying database, including database names, table structures, column names, and all stored data (e.g., user credentials, order details, product information). Complete database compromise is possible, leading to potential data exfiltration and unauthorized access.
findings.recommendation: Implement parameterized queries (prepared statements) for all database interactions. Never concatenate user-supplied input directly into SQL queries. Enforce strict input validation and sanitization on all user input. Consider deploying a Web Application Firewall (WAF) to detect and block common injection attempts. Regularly update and patch all database and application components.

findings.title: Default Admin Credentials Found
findings.description: The Metasploit auxiliary module `auxiliary/scanner/http/generic_login_bruteforce` successfully identified default or weak administrative credentials for the Juice Shop application. The credentials 'admin@juice-sh.op' and 'admin123' were found to be valid, granting full administrative access to the application. This vulnerability allows an attacker to bypass authentication and gain control over the application.
findings.recommendation: Immediately change the default administrative credentials ('admin@juice-sh.op' / 'admin123') to a strong, unique password. Implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) for administrative accounts. Regularly audit user accounts and remove any default or unused accounts. Enforce a strong password policy for all users.
findings.poc: hydra -L <path_to_user_list>/juice_shop_users.txt -P <path_to_password_list>/juice_shop_passwords.txt -s 443 -vV juice-shop.herokuapp.com http-post-form "/rest/user/login:{"email":"^USER^","password":"^PASS^"}:H=Content-Type: application/json:F=Invalid email or password."

findings.title: TLS 1.0
findings.description: The server supports TLS 1.0, an outdated and insecure version of the Transport Layer Security protocol. TLS 1.0 is vulnerable to various attacks, including BEAST and POODLE, and does not meet current security standards. Its use can expose sensitive data to eavesdropping and manipulation.
findings.recommendation: Disable TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 support on the server. Configure the server to only support TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 to ensure strong cryptographic protection and compliance with modern security best practices.

findings.title: Dev Subdomain Discovered
findings.description: A development subdomain, `dev.juice-shop.herokuapp.com`, was discovered via passive subdomain enumeration. Development environments often contain sensitive information, unpatched vulnerabilities, or relaxed security controls that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access to internal systems, source code, or proprietary data. This could also expose internal IP addresses or infrastructure details not intended for public disclosure.
findings.recommendation: Investigate the purpose and contents of the `dev.juice-shop.herokuapp.com` subdomain. If it's not intended for public access, restrict its visibility using network access controls (e.g., VPN, IP whitelisting) or strong authentication. Ensure it does not contain any sensitive data, exposed credentials, or exploitable configurations. If no longer needed, it should be decommissioned.

findings.title: CORS Wildcard Origin Misconfiguration
findings.description: The server responds with an 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *' header, indicating a Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) policy that allows any domain to access resources from this endpoint. If sensitive data or user-specific information is exposed via this API, it could be retrieved by arbitrary malicious websites, bypassing the same-origin policy.
findings.recommendation: Restrict the 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header to a whitelist of specific, trusted domains that are authorized to access the resources. Avoid using '*' unless the resource is truly public and contains no sensitive information. If credentials are used ('Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true'), browsers will typically not allow 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *'.

findings.title: S3 Bucket Publicly Readable
findings.description: An Amazon S3 bucket used for static assets (e.g., CSS, JS, images) for juice-shop.herokuapp.com is configured for public read access. While often intended for static content, this can expose sensitive files if misconfigured or if non-static content is accidentally placed within.
findings.recommendation: Review the bucket policy and ACLs. If public access is necessary for static content, ensure only intended files are public. Consider using CloudFront with Origin Access Control (OAC) to restrict direct S3 access.

findings.title: GCP Cloud Storage Bucket World Readable
findings.description: A Google Cloud Storage bucket named 'juice-shop-backup-data' has 'allUsers' or 'allAuthenticatedUsers' granted 'storage.objects.get' permission, making its contents publicly readable. This bucket appears to contain application backups, which could include sensitive configuration, user data, or source code.
findings.recommendation: Remove public access from the bucket. Ensure that only authorized service accounts or specific users/groups have access. Implement principle of least privilege for all storage buckets.

findings.title: EC2 Security Group Wide Open SSH
findings.description: An EC2 instance associated with the juice-shop application has a security group (sg-0abcdef1234567890) allowing SSH (port 22) access from '0.0.0.0/0' (anywhere on the internet). This significantly increases the risk of brute-force attacks and unauthorized access to the instance.
findings.recommendation: Restrict SSH ingress to specific trusted IP addresses or ranges. Consider using AWS Systems Manager Session Manager for secure shell access without opening inbound ports on security groups.

findings.title: IAM Role Over-privileged for S3 Access
findings.description: The IAM role 'juice-shop-backend-ec2-role', attached to EC2 instances running the application backend, has a policy granting 's3:*' permissions. This allows the role to perform any S3 action on any bucket in the account, violating the principle of least privilege. If the EC2 instance is compromised, an attacker could gain full control over all S3 data.
findings.recommendation: Refine the IAM policy to grant only the necessary S3 permissions (e.g., 's3:GetObject' on specific buckets) that the application requires for its functionality. Avoid using '*' for actions and resources.

findings.title: Unencrypted AWS RDS Database Instance
findings.description: The Amazon RDS database instance 'juice-shop-database-prod', which likely stores sensitive application data, is not configured with encryption at rest. In the event of underlying storage compromise, data could be exposed without encryption protection.
findings.recommendation: Enable encryption at rest for the RDS instance. This typically involves creating a snapshot of the unencrypted instance, restoring it to a new, encrypted instance, and then updating the application to connect to the new encrypted endpoint.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL Injection via product search
findings.description: The product search functionality at juice-shop.herokuapp.com is vulnerable to SQL injection, allowing an attacker to bypass authentication, extract sensitive data from the database, or manipulate application behavior.
findings.recommendation: Implement parameterized queries or prepared statements for all database interactions. Validate and sanitize all user inputs rigorously before use in database queries.
findings.poc: GET /rest/products/search?q=a%27%20OR%201%3D1-- (Observe all products returned, including potentially hidden ones)

findings.title: Critical vulnerability in Node.js dependency 'lodash'
findings.description: The 'lodash' package (version < 4.17.21), identified within the juice-shop application's dependencies, contains a prototype pollution vulnerability (CVE-2020-8203) that could lead to arbitrary code execution or denial of service.
findings.recommendation: Upgrade the 'lodash' dependency to version 4.17.21 or higher. Review 'package.json' and 'package-lock.json' for all dependencies.
findings.poc: Trivy output shows 'CVE-2022-XXXXX (HIGH) lodash Prototype Pollution' in the scan results.

findings.title: K8s Pod running with default service account and mounted token
findings.description: The Kubernetes pod running the juice-shop application is configured to use the default service account, and its service account token is automatically mounted inside the pod. If the application is compromised, an attacker could leverage this token to interact with the Kubernetes API, potentially escalating privileges within the cluster.
findings.recommendation: Configure the juice-shop deployment to use a dedicated service account with minimal necessary permissions. Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` in the pod's security context if no Kubernetes API access is required from within the pod.
findings.poc: kubectl exec -it <juice-shop-pod-name> -- cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token (Shows token present in pod)

findings.title: BOLA / IDOR
findings.description: The API endpoint `/api/v1/users/{id}` is vulnerable to Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA), also known as Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR). An authenticated attacker can manipulate the user ID in the URL path to access and retrieve sensitive profile information (e.g., email address, role) of any other user without proper authorization checks. This allows for unauthorized data exposure across user accounts.
findings.recommendation: Implement robust authorization checks on all API endpoints that access resources based on an ID. Before returning any data, the server must verify that the authenticated user is authorized to access the specific resource identified by the ID. This typically involves comparing the requested resource's owner ID with the currently authenticated user's ID or checking for administrative privileges. Additionally, consider using unpredictable identifiers (e.g., UUIDs) instead of sequential integers for sensitive resources.

findings.title: AWS Key Leak
findings.description: An AWS Access Key ID and Secret Access Key were found exposed within a publicly accessible '.env' file. This leak grants an attacker programmatic access to the AWS account, potentially allowing them to manage resources, exfiltrate data, incur unauthorized charges, or deploy malicious infrastructure. The detected keys are common example values, but their presence in a publicly accessible file indicates a critical misconfiguration.
findings.recommendation: Immediately revoke and rotate any compromised AWS keys. Implement a robust secret management solution (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault) and ensure that sensitive credentials are never stored directly in code repositories or exposed via publicly accessible files. Utilize IAM roles for applications running on AWS services instead of static credentials. Configure web servers to deny access to sensitive configuration files like '.env' and ensure they are not deployed to production environments.

findings.title: Cloudflare WAF Detected
findings.description: Cloudflare is a popular CDN and web security company that provides various services, including a Web Application Firewall (WAF). Its presence indicates that the application's traffic is being filtered and protected against common web attacks such as SQL injection, XSS, and DDoS. Cloudflare acts as a reverse proxy, inspecting incoming requests and outgoing responses.
findings.recommendation: While Cloudflare provides a strong layer of defense, it's crucial to ensure the application itself is secure. Regularly review Cloudflare WAF rules, monitor logs for blocked requests, and perform security testing (e.g., penetration testing) to identify vulnerabilities that might bypass the WAF or exist deeper within the application logic. Ensure the WAF rules are configured optimally for the specific application to prevent both false positives and unmitigated threats.

findings.title: SMB Null Session (Hypothetical)
findings.description: While juice-shop.herokuapp.com is a web application and does not expose SMB services directly, this finding simulates a scenario where an SMB null session vulnerability could be discovered on a related or co-located Windows host within the same network segment. An anonymous (null) session would allow enumeration of shared resources without authentication, leading to potential information disclosure.
findings.recommendation: Ensure no Windows servers or workstations within the organization's network allow anonymous (null) SMB sessions. Restrict anonymous access, enforce strong authentication for all SMB shares, and regularly audit share permissions. Consider using a firewall to block SMB ports (139, 445) from untrusted networks.

findings.title: Subdomain Takeover
findings.description: A dangling CNAME record for `shop.juice-shop.herokuapp.com` points to `non-existent-app-for-takeover-123.herokuapp.com`, which is an unclaimed Heroku application name. An attacker can register this Heroku application name and claim ownership of the subdomain `shop.juice-shop.herokuapp.com`, potentially hosting malicious content, phishing pages, or exploiting cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities under the legitimate domain's context.
findings.recommendation: Remove the CNAME record for `shop.juice-shop.herokuapp.com` if it is no longer in use. If the subdomain is intended to be active, update the CNAME record to point to an active and owned Heroku application, or another service that is fully controlled. Regularly audit DNS records to ensure all CNAMEs point to active and secured services.
